Putting the matter somewhat differently, in the instant case, the payer (i.e., the appellant) was expending public money (as it was statutorily obliged to do) to fund projects for the benefit of the public (who were the beneficiaries thereof either wholly or substantially), said projects being undertaken by the payees (i.e., the licensees). When considered from this perspective in our view the question requiring resolution becomes the following: is a payer, in respect of payments made under a contract which is entirely or substantially to the benefit of third parties unrelated to the payer (and being, as here, the public at large), obligated to deduct advance tax in terms of clause (b) of s. 153(1)?

To address this question, the relevant portion of subsection (1) may be stated as follows (emphasis supplied): “Every prescribed person making a payment … to a resident person … for the rendering of or providing of services…” shall deduct tax at the specified rate. It is important to keep in mind that s. 153(1) applies to transactions and situations that have not been randomly or haphazardly gathered together in one place. Rather, they are those that move within a certain legal framework. That frame is provided by the law of contracts, which constitutes the necessary legal backdrop in light of which the application of the section is to be considered. Once this is recognized then, in the specific context of clause (b), the contractual framework can be regarded as comprising of different elements. One is the services that have to be provided or rendered. There is then the person who provides or renders the services. Thirdly, there is the person -:35:- who makes payment for the services. Fourthly, there is the person for whom the services are being provided or rendered, i.e., to whose benefit they enure. Finally, there is the payment itself.

Learned counsel for the Department submits that it suffices, for purposes of making s. 153(1)(b) applicable, to identify the payer only in its capacity as the originator of the payment. Once, in addition to that, the recipient of the payment (i.e., the payee) is determined and it is confirmed that the payment is “for” the rendering or providing of services, that concludes the matter for purposes of the section. It matters not who is to benefit from the services being provided or rendered, i.e., whether it is the payer or some third party beneficiary. In other words, the recipient(s) of the services being provided or rendered is/are of no relevance. They simply need not be taken into account. In this sense even the payer is not relevant. Once the payment and its originator (i.e., the payer) are identified and linked in the specified way (by reason of the “for”) to the payee, the section becomes applicable; if the payer does not make the required deduction it becomes liable accordingly. On this basis, it is contended that the appellant was obligated to deduct tax on the payments made and, having failed to do so, must face the consequences including the application of s. 21(c). The approach advocated by learned counsel is certainly one interpretation. But it is not, with respect, the only sense in which s. 153(1)(b) can be understood. There is another sense, in which the “for” may be regarded as operating differently. For convenience, the approach urged by learned counsel for the Department is herein after referred to as the “first sense”, while the other, examined below, is referred to as the “second sense”.

In the second sense the section is attracted, and the obligation to deduct triggered, for payments made by the payer to the payee “for” providing or rendering services to the payer. This sense recognizes that the rendering or providing of services can have meaning only if it is also determined as to whom they are being provided or rendered. Of course in the vast majority of cases, the contractual rights, obligations and benefits move only between the parties thereto. The payer is both the recipient of the services (i.e., to whom they are provided or rendered), the -:36:- beneficiary thereof, and the one paying for the same. In such situations, there is complete identity between the two senses in which the “for” can be understood and applied. They are aligned. Ordinarily therefore, the legal backdrop in which s. 153(1)(b) operates, howsoever viewed, produces the same result insofar as the application of the section is concerned. However, once third party beneficiaries are introduced into the matrix (and such contracts would only be a small minority of cases), there can be disconnect between the one paying for the rendering or providing of services and the one to whom they are being rendered or provided. In such a situation the “for” operates in the second sense. The section would not be applicable, since in this sense the obligation to deduct arises only if the services are being provided or rendered to the payer. That however would not be the situation. The second sense can, in a way, be regarded as being even more literal than the first sense. This is because in the first sense the phrase “rendering of or providing of services” is, really speaking, shorthand for referring to the contractual obligations of the payee. Here, the “for” merely links the contractual obligations on the two sides. On the side of the payer, that obligation is the payment while on the side of the payee it is the rendering or providing of services. The section is triggered when the obligor on one side (the payer) discharges his obligation (i.e., makes the payment) to the obligor on the other side (the payee). In this sense, who is the recipient of those services (i.e., to whom the benefit thereof is directed or accrues) is of no moment. As noted, this is the sense that is pressed by learned counsel for the Department. However, when the provision is read even more literally than that, i.e., in the second sense, then the “for” links not the contractual obligations on the two sides but the recipients (respectively) of the payment and the services rendered or provided. In this sense the section applies to what actually flows under the contract, i.e., the payment and the services, and to whom. It is therefore triggered only when the payer is the recipient of the services being rendered or provided.

As already noted, in the vast majority of transactions and situations the two senses produce the same result because the rights and obligations of the parties (howsoever viewed), and the -:37:- benefits accruing or flowing from the one to the other (again, howsoever viewed) remain only inter se. They merge into each other. However one approaches the section, the position remains the same and, therefore, so does the obligation of the payer to deduct tax. But when third party beneficiaries are involved there is a divergence. If the section is applied in the first sense it results in the obligation to deduct arising. However, if applied in the second sense there is no obligation to deduct. This is because there the requirement that the payer be the recipient of the payee’s obligation (i.e., the one who obtains the benefit of, or accruing or flowing from, the providing or rendering of services) is not met. The recipient is the third party beneficiary. In our view both senses of interpreting and applying s. 153(2)(b) are reasonable. Again, this is because it must be remembered at all times that the section operates in the legal framework provided by the law of contracts. In the first sense, that backdrop is a contract where the rights and obligations, and the benefits of and from the contract, are only between the parties. In the second sense, the backdrop changes and third party beneficiaries are also within the contract. In the former, there is undoubtedly the obligation to deduct tax on the payer. However, in the second there ought not to be any such obligation, for the reasons set out in para 37 above. The contracts at hand fall in the latter category, especially when, as a matter of fact, the third party beneficiaries here are the public at large. The appellant is not the recipient of the services rendered or provided by the licensee. The second sense prevails.

Before concluding, one point may be made. We recognize that there can be a difference between the providing or rendering of a service and the benefits flowing or accruing in terms thereof. (Again, it must be remembered that this would be an unusual and atypical situation.) The services may be provided or rendered to one who is party to the contract while the benefits accrue or arise to one who is not. If that were so then it may be erroneous to conflate the two. In the case at hand, however, the contracts were entered into to give effect to “special projects”, i.e., in order to provide telecommunication services to unserved or underserved areas. It was in the very nature of such services that they were intended for (indeed, could only be provided to) the residents of -:38:- such areas, i.e., the third party beneficiaries being the public at large. They could not ipso facto be provided or rendered to the appellant. Thus, the difference under consideration in this para did not arise in the facts and circumstances of the case. Both the persons to whom the services were being provided or rendered and those obtaining the benefit thereof were the same, and not the appellant.

In view of the foregoing discussion and analysis the question posed in para 41 is answered in the negative. The appellant was not under an obligation to deduct tax under s. 153(2)(b). Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The impugned decision of the ADR Committee is set aside as is the amending order, to the extent here relevant. It is declared that s. 21(c) had no application to the facts and circumstances of the case.
